nameStory: This microscopic algae gets its name from the Greek words 'eu' meaning 'good' or 'well' and 'astron' meaning 'star,' referring to its beautiful star-like symmetrical shape when viewed under a microscope. The species name 'oblongum' comes from Latin meaning 'oblong' or 'elongated,' describing its stretched-out oval outline that's longer than it is wide.
description: Euastrum oblongum is a single-celled freshwater algae called a desmid that's invisible to the naked eye but reveals incredible beauty under a microscope. Each cell looks like a tiny green hourglass or figure-eight, divided into two mirror-image halves called semicells that are perfectly symmetrical. These microscopic organisms are typically about 140-180 micrometers long (roughly twice the width of a human hair) and live floating freely in clean pond and lake water. Despite being single cells, they have complex shapes with lobes, notches, and small bumps that make them look like miniature works of art.

idTips.label: Hourglass Shape
idTips.description: The cell has a distinctive figure-eight or hourglass outline with a narrow waist (called the isthmus) connecting two identical halves

idTips.label: Lobed Semicells
idTips.description: Each half of the cell has four distinct lobes - two at the base and two on the sides - that appear doubled due to shallow indentations or 'pits'

idTips.label: Notched Top
idTips.description: The top of each semicell is flattened (truncate) with a deep V-shaped notch cut into it, like a tiny green crown

idTips.label: Surface Bumps
idTips.description: Small rounded protuberances (bumps) are visible on the cell surface - one above the waist, two in the center, and one in each lobe

idTips.label: Green Coloration
idTips.description: The cell appears bright green under the microscope due to its chloroplasts (the parts that capture sunlight for photosynthesis)

habitat: You'll find this microscopic algae floating in clean, moderately nutrient-rich (mesotrophic) ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. It prefers waters that aren't too polluted but have enough nutrients to support plant life - often in bog ponds, woodland pools, and the quieter edges of larger lakes. To observe it, you'll need to collect a water sample and examine it under a microscope with at least 100x magnification.

seasonality.spring: As water temperatures warm, populations begin to increase and are often easiest to find in shallow, sun-warmed areas of ponds and lakes where they actively photosynthesize.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm months when water temperatures and sunlight are optimal for growth and reproduction through cell division.
seasonality.fall: Populations remain active but may begin to decline as temperatures drop and daylight hours decrease, though they can still be found in suitable waters.
seasonality.winter: Present but less active in ice-free waters or under ice cover, with reduced populations that survive until spring warming triggers new growth.

funFact: Despite being a single cell, Euastrum oblongum is essentially immortal - it reproduces by splitting perfectly in half, with each half regenerating the missing portion, meaning there's no natural death from old age, only from environmental factors or predation!
confusionNotes: It's most easily confused with other Euastrum species that share the same basic hourglass shape, but you can distinguish E. oblongum by counting its lobes (four per semicell with shallow pits) and looking for the specific pattern of surface bumps. Remember: 'Oblong oblongum' - it's more stretched out lengthwise than many of its rounder relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Desmids like Euastrum are considered 'living jewels' by microscopists and are prized for their perfect symmetry and intricate beauty. They're important indicators of water quality - finding diverse desmid populations usually means you're looking at clean, healthy aquatic ecosystems, making them nature's tiny environmental report cards.
compareHints: Euastrum oblongum differs from its relatives by its distinctly oblong (elongated) outline and specific lobe pattern - E. bidentatum has fewer, more tooth-like projections, while E. denticulatum has more numerous small teeth around its edges. Unlike the heavily ornamented E. verrucosum with its warty surface, E. oblongum has a relatively smooth appearance with just a few strategic bumps, making it one of the more 'streamlined' members of its genus.
